26. TDS ON DIVIDEND PAID TO SHAREHOLDER / MEMBER
For Resident Shareholder / Member

For Resident Shareholder / Member
Under section 393(1) of the Income Tax Act 2025, the Company is required to deduct tax at source on any dividend paid or credited to a resident shareholder, at the rates in force as per the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 2026.
However as per the current law (successor to the first proviso to section 194 of the 1961 Act), no TDS will be deducted where the shareholder is a resident individual, and the aggregate amount of dividend to be paid or credited by the Company during the Financial Year 2026-27 does not exceed ` 10,000.
Further, if the resident individual / HUF member provides duly signed declaration in Form 121 (erstwhile form 15G/ Form 15H) (as applicable), no TDS shall be applicable provided that the eligibility conditions are being met.
In accordance with the current statutory provisions, TDS shall be deducted at a higher rate of 20% if:
1. The member's valid PAN is not registered or available with the Company or Depository Participant.
2. The registered PAN is invalid or inoperative due to non-compliance with the statutory PAN–Aadhaar linking mandates under the 2025 Act framework. Members are strongly advised to ensure their PAN–Aadhaar link is active to avoid this higher deduction.
TDS Rates applicable to Resident Shareholder: -
Members having valid PAN 10% or as notified by the Government of India

Members having valid PAN 10% or as notified by the Government of India
20% or as notified by the Government of India
Members not having PAN / valid PAN / PAN not linked with Aadhaar, as applicable
Shareholders who are required to link Aadhaar with PAN under section 262(5)–(7) read with Rule 162 are strongly advised to ensure that their PAN is operative by the record date, to avoid higher TDS.
For Non - Resident Shareholder / Member
As per Section 393(2) of the Income Tax Act, 2025 the rate of withholding tax is 20% (plus applicable surcharge and cess). However, where a non-resident member is eligible to claim the tax treaty benefit, and the tax rate provided in the respective tax treaty is beneficial to the Member, then the rate as per the tax treaty would be applied. In order to avail tax treaty benefits, non-resident shareholders would be required to submit all the below documents:
• Tax Residency Certificate for Tax Year 2026-27, the year in which the dividend is received (to be obtained from the Revenue / Tax authorities of the country of which the shareholder is resident)
• E-filed Form 41 Duly filled and electronically generated via the Indian Income Tax Department’s e-filing portal under Section 159(8)(b) and Rule 75 of the Income Tax Rules, 2026. Copy of PAN Card if available
• Self-declaration of beneficial ownership and not having a Permanent Establishment in India

• Self-declaration of beneficial ownership and not having a Permanent Establishment in India
All the aforesaid documents can be submitted at following link:
https://ris.kfintech.com/form15/default.aspx
The application of beneficial DTAA rates is not automatic. It is subject to the completeness, compliance, and satisfactory legal review of the submitted documents by the Company.
For All Members
In accordance with rule 203 of Income Tax Rules, 2026, where shares are held by intermediaries / stock brokers, then such intermediaries / stock brokers can provide the details of such beneficial members along with self-declaration that the shareholders are the beneficial owners. Hence, the TDS will be applied by the Company on the PAN of the beneficial members.

In terms of Rule 203 of Income Tax Rules 2026, if dividend income on which tax has been deducted at source is assessable in the hands of a person other than the registered Member, then such registered Member should furnish a declaration containing the name, address, PAN of the person to whom TDS credit is to be given, proportion of credit and reasons for giving credit to such person with the Company in the manner prescribed by the Rules. Such declarations under Rule 203, need to be submitted on or before Tuesday, September 1, 2026 for enabling the Company to consider the same. Any request submitted after the record date shall not be considered.
Please also note that in order to claim credit of TDS deducted by Glenmark Pharmaceuticals Limited, it is mandatory to have valid PAN updated at depository’s register. The Company shall not be held liable for unavailability of TDS credit due to invalid / incorrect PAN available in depository’s record. Further, member is required to submit relevant declarations / documents mentioned above on or before Tuesday, September 1, 2026, in order to avail benefit of lower / Nil rate.
Forms are available on https://ris.kfintech.com/form15/default.aspx members may also submit any other document as prescribed under the Income Tax Act to claim a lower / Nil withholding tax.

Forms are available on https://ris.kfintech.com/form15/default.aspx members may also submit any other document as prescribed under the Income Tax Act to claim a lower / Nil withholding tax.

Mrs. Blanche E. Saldanha (aged 86 years) is a Non-Executive Director and a member of the promoter group of Glenmark Pharmaceuticals Limited. About Glenmark
A New Way for A New World
Through our biotech arm, Ichnos Glenmark Innovation (IGI), and a robust network of global in- licensing and strategic partnerships, we are building a pipeline of differentiated and globally relevant therapies. Innovation at Glenmark extends across the value chain: from science and development to access, partnerships, and delivery.

Glenmark Pharmaceuticals Limited is a global pharmaceutical company headquartered in Mumbai, India, with a presence in over 80 countries. The Company is entering its next phase of growth as a more focused, innovation-led, and globally relevant pharmaceutical enterprise built on strong commercial platforms, differentiated science, manufacturing excellence, and strategic partnerships.
We are equally defined by purpose. Aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs), Glenmark continues to advance environmental and social priorities with discipline and accountability. We are a water-positive organization, among the first pharmaceutical companies globally to align with the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) framework, and our climate goals have been validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). Through our social responsibility initiatives, we have positively impacted over 5.8 Mn lives across maternal and child health, livelihoods, education, the promotion of swimming as a sport, and other priority areas of sustainable development.

Our portfolio spans branded, innovative, generics, and consumer products, supported by deep therapeutic expertise and a strong commercial presence across India, North America, Europe, Latin America, Asia Pacific, Russia and the CIS, the Middle East, and Africa. With 11 world-class manufacturing sites and six cutting-edge R&D centers, we deliver high-quality medicines that are accessible across categories and geographies, while upholding rigorous standards of quality, compliance, and supply reliability.
At the heart of Glenmark’s strategy is a clear therapeutic focus on Respiratory, Dermatology, and Oncology. These are the areas where we combine scientific depth, commercial agility, and patient-centric execution to address unmet patient needs at scale. This focus is enabling Glenmark to move decisively up the value chain from established strengths in branded and generics portfolio towards differentiated and innovation-led opportunities.
Glenmark is building its next chapter, anchored in science, strengthened by global execution, and powered by impact.
This is Glenmark: A New Way for A New World.

At Glenmark, innovation is driven by a clear purpose: to advance differentiated, science-led therapies that address significant unmet health needs and create meaningful impact for patients.
Through Ichnos Glenmark Innovation (IGI), Glenmark is building a proprietary biologics innovation engine focused on next-generation multispecific antibodies. Powered by the BEAT® platform, IGI is developing immune-cell engagers and modulators designed to address complex cancers through differentiated mechanisms of action.
Our innovation pipeline reflects this ambition. It brings together proprietary discovery, next- generation biologics, strategic partnerships, and disciplined development capabilities to build a portfolio that is scientifically differentiated, globally relevant, and commercially meaningful.
The licensing of ISB 2001, now ABBV-2001, to AbbVie marked a defining validation of this platform and of Glenmark’s long-term investment in original innovation. The agreement gives AbbVie rights across North America, Europe, Japan, and Greater China, with IGI having received an upfront payment of USD 700 Mn and eligible to receive USD 1.225 Bn in milestone payments and tiered double-digit royalties.

Building Higher-Quality Growth
Our ambition is not simply greater scale, but growth of greater quality, differentiation, and durability.
The Glenmark emerging today combines the reach and execution capabilities of a global pharmaceutical company with a growing ability to originate, access, partner, and commercialize differentiated science. We are now turning these strengths together with greater consistency, discipline, and ambition. That, to me, is the real meaning of Redefining the Future.

Ryaltris® is one of the clearest examples. Developed through Glenmark’s proprietary research and development (R&D) capabilities, it has progressed from internal innovation into a global respiratory brand with approvals and commercialization across a growing number of markets. It demonstrates our ability to originate an asset, advance it through global regulatory pathways, create a compelling therapeutic proposition and deploy the right commercial model across markets.

India, North America, Europe, and Emerging Markets provide diversification, therapeutic depth, market access, and the ability to operate across healthcare systems with very different needs and dynamics. During FY2026, we continued to strengthen these businesses while improving the quality of the portfolio we bring through them.
As we build the next phase of Glenmark, we will create value through multiple innovation models. We will originate proprietary assets where our science can create meaningful differentiation, partner our innovation where global development capabilities can accelerate its potential, and bring compelling external science into markets where Glenmark has the therapeutic expertise and commercial infrastructure to realize its potential.

India remains one of our most important growth engines. Where Capabilities Converge
Healthcare is entering one of the most dynamic periods in its history. New modalities are changing drug discovery and development, while AI and data science are reshaping how targets are identified, trials are designed, and evidence is generated. At the same time, healthcare systems worldwide must reconcile the pace of innovation with affordability, access, and sustainability.

What comes next matters greatly. ISB 2301, ISB 2302, and ISB 2501 represent the next wave of multispecific programs, alongside partnered programs in Immunology. Each is at an earlier stage and carries the scientific and clinical risk inherent in drug development. Our ambition is to build a stronger and increasingly repeatable innovation engine.
This environment will reward companies capable of connecting capabilities that have historically operated separately.
Glenmark’s commercial businesses give us reach; our therapeutic strengths give us depth; our proprietary products demonstrate our ability to innovate and commercialize; our partnerships broaden the science we can bring to patients; IGI extends our participation at the frontiers of multispecific innovation; and our stronger financial position gives us the capacity to invest deliberately behind these opportunities.
The model is clear: create differentiated science, advance it to meaningful validation, partner where the right global capabilities can accelerate development, and reinvest in the next generation of innovation. ISB 2001 should not be seen as the culmination of our innovation journey. It should raise the starting point for what comes next.

Board Architecture and Diversity
Strategic Oversight and Risk Governance

Strategic Oversight and Risk Governance
Glenmark’s Board combines executive knowledge with independent judgement and diverse professional experience. The Board brings together expertise across pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, finance, and global business, ensuring balanced oversight, strong governance, and informed decision-making.
The Board oversees Glenmark’s strategy, capital allocation, and risk framework, informed by business performance, market dynamics, scientific and regulatory developments, and stakeholder expectations. As the Company advances across the Base Business, Innovation/Specialty, and IGI, the Board evaluates investments in differentiated products, innovative assets, biologics, manufacturing, partnerships, and global infrastructure. The Risk Management Committee supports oversight of principal and emerging risks, while management remains accountable for risk mitigation, monitoring, execution, business continuity, and resilience across global operations.
Familiarization Program for Directors
The Company conducts familiarization programs to deepen Directors’ understanding of the business, its operating environment, and governance practices. Regular engagement with the business and senior leadership enables Directors to have informed oversight and effective decision-making.
Internal Control and Assurance

Internal Control and Assurance
Glenmark maintains a robust internal control framework encompassing financial, operational, quality, compliance, and IT controls. The framework is designed to support reliable reporting, safeguard assets, enable compliance with applicable requirements and promote effective business operations. Continuous monitoring and independent assurance activities strengthen governance, support risk mitigation, and enable informed decision-making across the business. The Audit Committee provides focused oversight of financial reporting, internal controls and assurance processes. It reviews matters raised by internal and statutory auditors and monitors management actions arising from audit findings.
Succession and Leadership Continuity
Succession planning is an integral part of Glenmark’s governance framework. The Board and management periodically review leadership requirements and talent pipelines to support continuity and organizational resilience. Leadership development, internal mobility, and external talent assessment support the creation of a sustainable pipeline across business and functional roles.

Ethics, Integrity, and Speak-Up Culture
Regulatory Compliance

Regulatory Compliance
Ethical conduct is fundamental to stakeholder trust and responsible business performance. Glenmark’s policies establish clear expectations for Directors, employees, and relevant business partners and provide mechanisms through which concerns can be raised, investigated, and addressed.
Glenmark operates across multiple jurisdictions and is subject to extensive legal, regulatory, quality, and industry requirements. Compliance responsibilities are embedded across business and functional teams, supported by policies, SOPs, monitoring, and escalation mechanisms.
The Code of Conduct forms the foundation of Glenmark’s ethical framework. It sets out the principles and standards expected across areas including integrity, fairness, conflicts of interest, responsible business practices, and compliance with applicable laws and policies.
Related-Party Transactions
All related-party transactions are conducted on an arm’s length basis and in the ordinary course of business, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations. The Audit Committee provides oversight to ensure transparency, fairness, and protection of stakeholder interests.
Communication, training and leadership reinforcement support the application of these principles in everyday decision-making across the organization.
Sustainability and ESG Oversight
Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption

Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption
Oversight of ESG priorities is integrated into Glenmark’s governance architecture. The ESG Committee provides focused oversight of the Company’s sustainability priorities, commitments, and performance and supports the integration of material ESG considerations into business decisions.
Glenmark maintains a zero-tolerance approach toward bribery and corruption. The Anti-Bribery and Anti- Corruption Policy provides guidance on preventing, identifying, escalating, and reporting improper conduct across the jurisdictions in which the Company operates.
Shareholder Stewardship
Glenmark is committed to transparent communication, equitable treatment, and active engagement with shareholders. We provide efficient mechanisms for voting, grievance redressal, and timely access to information, while safeguarding shareholder interests.
Vigil Mechanism and Whistle-Blower Policy
This provides channels through which employees and other stakeholders can report suspected misconduct, unethical behavior or violations of law and policy.
Board Evaluation

Board Evaluation
Concerns may be raised through established reporting mechanisms and are assessed through defined investigation and escalation processes. The framework includes safeguards against retaliation for concerns raised in good faith, reinforcing a culture in which individuals are expected to act responsibly and are encouraged to speak up.
The Board, its Committees, and individual Directors undergo an annual evaluation to assess their effectiveness, governance practices, and strategic oversight. The process supports continuous improvement, accountability, and enhanced Board performance.

Expanding Access to Next-Generation EGFR-Targeted Therapy
In September 2025, Glenmark entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with Hengrui Pharma for Trastuzumab Rezetecan (SHR-A1811), a next- generation HER2-targeting Antibody-Drug Conjugate (ADC). Under the agreement, Glenmark secured exclusive rights to develop and commercialize Trastuzumab Rezetecan across multiple global markets, excluding Mainland China, the Hong Kong SAR, the Macao SAR, Taiwan Region, the U.S., Canada, Europe, Japan, and Russia and the CIS.

In FY2026, Glenmark announced a partnership with Hansoh Pharma to develop and commercialize Aumolertinib across the Middle East and Africa, Southeast and South Asia, India, Australia, New Zealand, Russia/CIS and select Caribbean countries. The agreement gives Glenmark exclusive rights to develop and commercialize Aumolertinib across these licensed territories.
Aumolertinib is a third-generation Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It is designed to target EGFR-driven disease and address a significant treatment need in NSCLC.
Trastuzumab Rezetecan, currently approved for unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic HER2- positive NSCLC and in HER2-positive second-line breast cancer in China, has further been included in the NMPA’s Breakthrough Therapy Designation list for nine indications, covering NSCLC, breast cancer, gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, biliary tract cancer, and gynecologic malignancies.

Aumolertinib is marketed as Ameile® in China and approved in the United Kingdom and Europe, where it is indicated for the first-line treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with activating EGFR mutations, and the treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic EGFR T790M mutation-positive NSCLC. Way Forward
Platform-Led Innovation Strategy
Over the next 12–18 months, IGI will focus on advancing its differentiated innovation pipeline while continuing to execute on its partnership-led model.

Over the next 12–18 months, IGI will focus on advancing its differentiated innovation pipeline while continuing to execute on its partnership-led model.
IGI’s pipeline strategy is anchored in its proprietary BEAT® antibody engineering platform. The platform enables the design of differentiated multispecific antibodies and supports exploration of multiple immune-cell engagement approaches, including T-cell and NK-cell engagers.
Key priorities include progressing ISB 2001/ABBV- 2001 in collaboration with AbbVie across licensed territories, supporting continued development in retained territories, and advancing the ongoing dose-expansion program towards dose optimization. IGI will also advance ISB 2301 through IND submission and towards First-in-Human development, while strengthening its next wave of multispecific candidates, including ISB 2302 and ISB 2501.
ISB 2301 is central to this next wave. By targeting three tumor-associated antigens and activating both T-cells and NK-cells, it is designed to address tumor heterogeneity, immune escape, and resistance pathways that remain major challenges in solid tumor oncology.
In parallel, IGI will support partner-led development of its Immunology assets and evaluate strategic collaborations that can accelerate pipeline value creation. Through this approach, IGI aims to build a globally relevant innovation portfolio that combines strong science, clinical differentiation, and long-term value creation for patients, partners, and shareholders.
IGI’s approach combines internal scientific innovation with a partnership-led value creation model. This enables the Company to advance differentiated assets, partner selectively at value-inflection points and continue investing in early-stage discovery and development.

We are committed to maintaining the highest standards of accountability and transparency in our tax practices, ensuring full compliance with all applicable laws and regulations. Our approach to taxation is grounded in a strong sense of responsibility, recognizing that our tax practices have implications not only for our business but also for the broader society and economies in which we operate. This commitment is reinforced through our Tax Policy, which mandates strict adherence to all relevant statutory requirements and promotes consistency and transparency in tax matters.
We are committed to advancing both our existing portfolio and next-generation therapies across key therapeutic areas. Our investments support the development of novel, high-value assets, while also driving continuous improvement in our current product range. This balanced approach enables us to deliver better patient outcomes globally while building a robust and future-ready business.

Our commitment extends beyond regulatory compliance. We proactively engage with tax authorities to address any potential discrepancies or disputes in a timely and constructive manner. Through open and transparent communication, we seek to build relationships based on mutual trust, respect, and a shared commitment to tax integrity. By embedding accountability and transparency into our tax practices, we reaffirm our role as a responsible corporate citizen and support the principles of sustainable and ethical business conduct. Advancing Our Manufacturing Facilities

At Glenmark, quality is fundamental to our purpose of improving patient outcomes and building trust across the healthcare ecosystem. We embed quality throughout the product lifecycle, from development and technology transfer to manufacturing, warehousing, distribution, and post-market surveillance, to ensure that every product consistently meets the highest standards of safety, efficacy, and regulatory compliance.

Maintaining inspection readiness and a strong compliance culture remains a strategic priority. Under our Corporate Internal Audit Framework, every manufacturing site undergoes comprehensive audits at least once every six months. These assessments are supplemented by surprise audits, for-cause audits, and periodic self-inspections to evaluate the effectiveness of site-level quality systems and ensure sustained compliance.
Our Integrated Quality Management System (IQMS) serves as the foundation of this commitment, providing a robust and globally harmonized framework that drives quality excellence across our operations. The system integrates standardized procedures, validated processes, continuous process verification, rigorous testing protocols, and risk-based quality oversight to ensure consistent product performance and regulatory compliance across markets.
During FY2026, our facilities underwent 30 internal audits and 37 regulatory inspections by health authorities across multiple markets.
Insights generated from these assessments are translated into targeted improvement initiatives covering process simplification, investigation effectiveness, deviation management, quality review mechanisms, data integrity enhancement, and quality system optimization.

Pharmacovigilance

Pharmacovigilance
At Glenmark, pharmacovigilance is an integral component of our commitment to patient safety, responsible healthcare, and product stewardship. Through a robust and globally integrated Pharmacovigilance (PV) framework, we continuously monitor the safety profile of our products throughout their lifecycle, enabling the timely identification, evaluation, and mitigation of emerging safety risks.
To facilitate timely reporting and effective safety monitoring, we offer multiple reporting channels, including toll-free helplines, dedicated pharmacovigilance email addresses, website-based reporting platforms, and direct reporting pathways through healthcare providers and business partners.
Our pharmacovigilance systems are aligned with Good Pharmacovigilance Practices (GVP), applicable local regulations, and international safety standards, ensuring that patient safety remains central to every stage of product commercialization and post-market monitoring.
All reported product safety events are captured within a validated global safety database, medically reviewed by qualified personnel, and reported to health authorities in accordance with applicable regulatory timelines.

ISB 2001/ABBV-2001 is being evaluated in the ongoing Phase 1 TRIgnite-1 study in patients with relapsed and/or refractory multiple myeloma. The program received Orphan Drug Designation from the U.S. FDA in July 2023 and Fast Track Designation in April 2025 for adult patients who had received at least three prior lines of therapy.
ISB 2001/ABBV-2001 is IGI’s lead investigational Oncology asset and the first oncology program developed using the proprietary BEAT® protein platform to show Proof of Concept and move into late-stage development.
The trispecific T-cell engager targets CD38 and BCMA on multiple myeloma cells and CD3 on T-cells. By engaging two tumor-associated antigens, the molecule is designed to increase recognition of myeloma cells across varying levels of target expression, while recruiting T-cells to support tumor-cell killing.
A Phase 1/2 multi-cohort combination study in multiple myeloma with other antimyeloma therapies has been initiated (NCT06892522).

ISB 830 (Telazorlimab) and the OX40 antagonist platform were licensed to Astria Therapeutics in October 2023. Telazorlimab is an OX40 antagonist that successfully completed a Phase 2B study in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis in 2021. Its follow-on molecule, ISB 830-X8, now known as STAR-0310, is being developed for atopic dermatitis and potentially other indications. STAR-0310 is a potential best- in-class, T-cell-sparing, immunomodulating OX40 antagonist designed to have a long half-life.

Potential suppliers undergo a structured evaluation of business capabilities, quality systems, regulatory compliance and operational performance. Combating Household Air Pollution
Around 2.1 Bn people globally continue to cook with open fires or inefficient stoves, resulting in an estimated 3.2 Mn deaths each year from household air pollution¹. In India, many households continue to cook with solid fuels on a daily basis, contributing to harmful indoor air pollution and posing health risks, particularly for women and children. To address this pressing issue, Glenmark Foundation collaborated with CSIR-NEERI to develop PAVAK, a low-cost, improved cookstove that has been extensively researched and field-tested.

Under the PAVAK Cookstove Project, we installed 15,700 smokeless cookstoves across 75 villages in the Akkalkuwa and Dhadgaon blocks of Nandurbar district, Maharashtra in FY2026. This directly supported our broader efforts to reduce indoor air pollution exposure for mothers and young children during cooking.

Enhancing Energy Efficiency Through Operational and Utility Optimization
Advancing Energy Efficiency Through Smart Utility and HVAC Management
At our Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (CSN) site, we improved energy efficiency by streamlining operations and optimizing utility systems. In the nasal production area, garment sterilization activities were discontinued, eliminating the need for energy- intensive sterilization equipment and associated utility consumption. We also implemented controlled shutdowns in non-operational production areas, reducing the operating hours of air handling systems and avoiding unnecessary energy use.

To strengthen operational sustainability and reduce energy consumption, the Sikkim facility implemented a series of energy-efficiency initiatives in FY2026 across utility, HVAC, and ventilation systems. The project focused on optimizing equipment performance through Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs), deployment of a heat pump for hot water generation, and timer-based control of ventilation motors. These interventions improved energy utilization without impacting process performance.
Further efficiencies were achieved by optimizing chilled water distribution and consolidating cooling tower operations, reducing the energy demand of cooling utilities. In addition, Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) were installed on chiller pumps, enabling them to operate according to actual cooling requirements rather than at constant speed. Together, these initiatives improved resource efficiency, reduced operating costs, and lowered the site’s environmental footprint.
Key measures included installing a VFD on the cooling tower pump to optimize motor load, replacing steam-based hot water generation with a heat pump, optimizing AHU motor speeds, and introducing timers to reduce unnecessary ventilation run-time. Together, these initiatives delivered significant reductions in electricity and fuel consumption while improving operational efficiency.

At our Nashik site, we implemented a range of energy conservation measures, including the procurement of solar power through open-access arrangements, the use of biofuels, improvements in bottle cleaning processes, enhanced efficiency of ETP dryer operations, and upgrades to HVAC systems. Together, these initiatives delivered annual electricity savings of more than 2 Mn kWh, while lowering operating costs and supporting our climate action goals.
The program achieved annual savings of approximately 1,46,000 kWh of electricity and 68,800 liters of fuel, generating annual cost savings of about INR 4.7 Mn. With an overall payback period of nearly one year, the project demonstrates how targeted energy-management measures can deliver both environmental and financial benefits while supporting long-term sustainability goals.

Water Stewardship Strategy
Our water management approach is anchored on four strategic pillars:
Reducing dependence on freshwater sources remains a core focus across facilities. We implement process optimization and deploy water-efficient technologies to minimize blue water use. Key initiatives include recovery and reuse of hot condensate through condensate recovery units, reuse of steam condensate as boiler feed water, and utilization of reverse osmosis (RO) reject water for domestic applications.
Reducing Blue Water Consumption
Automated sensors and flow control valves are installed in canteens and washrooms to prevent wastage, while treated effluent is reused for utilities, irrigation, and toilet flushing. Landscaping requirements are met through sprinkler-based irrigation systems, and rainwater harvesting structures are used to support groundwater recharge. Together, these measures significantly lower freshwater intake across operations.

To further enhance treatment efficiency and reuse potential, we continue to invest in water and wastewater infrastructure upgrades. This includes modernization of the primary treatment unit at Baddi, installation of Membrane Biological Reactor (MBR)- based STPs at Goa, Mahape, and Baddi, and deployment of ZLD units at Nashik, Sikkim, and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. These interventions strengthen our ability to recycle treated wastewater and reduce liquid discharge.
Infrastructure Strengthening for Water Sustainability
Responsible wastewater management is a critical component of our water stewardship framework. We have implemented Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems at 3 of our 8 manufacturing sites in India. At the remaining sites, treated effluent is recycled for non- potable applications such as gardening and toilet flushing. In FY2026, we recycled and reused 79% of wastewater generated across our Indian operations. This performance is supported by advanced Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs), Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs), and ZLD systems that ensure compliance with stringent pharmaceutical industry standards while minimizing environmental impact.

In FY2026, we became the first pharmaceutical company globally to publish a verified Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) report, covering all operational sites across India, the U.S., Argentina, and the Czech Republic. Through this assessment, we mapped each site’s ecological footprint against its surrounding biome and ecoregion, creating a robust evidence base to identify biodiversity-related dependencies, impacts, risks, and opportunities across our operations.
Our Approach to Biodiversity Management
Our biodiversity management approach begins with site mapping and ecosystem screening to assess biodiversity-related dependencies, impacts, and risks.
Using a risk-based methodology, we evaluated the proximity of all operational sites to Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) and critical habitats, enabling the prioritization of locations requiring enhanced biodiversity management.

Using a risk-based methodology, we evaluated the proximity of all operational sites to Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) and critical habitats, enabling the prioritization of locations requiring enhanced biodiversity management.
Our assessment combined sector-level and site-level analyses to ensure a comprehensive understanding of nature-related impacts. Using the ENCORE tool and WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter, we identified the pharmaceutical sector’s key dependencies and pressures on ecosystem services. We complemented this with site-specific assessments based on the World Resources Institute’s Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, evaluating provisioning, regulating, and cultural ecosystem services within a 10 km radius of each facility. Guided by the TNFD LEAP framework, Locate, Evaluate, Assess, and Prepare, we assessed all manufacturing facilities and R&D Centers along with their surrounding landscapes.
Based on this assessment, four sites – Sikkim, Nashik, Mahape, and the Czech Republic facility – were identified as priority locations.
A Biodiversity Management Plan was initially developed for Sikkim, and during FY2026, a comprehensive BMP was also completed for the Nashik facility, strengthening our site-specific approach to biodiversity stewardship.

Site-Level Biodiversity Management in Sikkim
At our Sikkim facility, biodiversity conservation is closely linked with water stewardship and climate resilience. The site sources spring water from the Rani Khola watershed and operates a zero-liquid- discharge system to optimize water use and reduce freshwater withdrawal.
During FY2026, we initiated a Spring Rejuvenation Project to support long-term water security, improve watershed health, and enhance ecosystem resilience in the region. Recognizing local climate and geological risks, including landslides and seismic activity, we aim to implement appropriate infrastructure and emergency preparedness measures, and afforestation initiatives in partnership with the Forest Department.
Biodiversity Management Plan

Biodiversity Management Plan
Following the development of our first Biodiversity Management Plan for Sikkim, we are progressively extending this site-specific framework across other priority locations. During FY2026, we developed and implemented a comprehensive Biodiversity Management Plan (BMP) for Nashik, outlining short-, medium-, and long-term actions to conserve biodiversity, enhance ecosystem services, and address site-specific nature-related risks.
As part of our conservation efforts, we partnered with the Forest Department to plant more than 400 saplings at Dari Matori, Nashik, contributing to ecosystem restoration, habitat enhancement, carbon sequestration, and landscape resilience.

Geopolitical and Technological Drivers
Geopolitical tensions, particularly the conflict in the Middle East, have increased downside risks by disrupting trade, logistics, and financial conditions. Further escalation, prolonged policy uncertainty or renewed market volatility could affect business confidence, investment, and cross-border activity. At the same time, continued investment in technology and artificial intelligence is expected to support productivity and strengthen long-term economic resilience.

Global growth is expected to remain subdued in 2026, reflecting elevated uncertainty and geopolitical risk. The World Bank and IMF project global GDP growth for 2026 in the range of 2.5% to 3.1%. Advanced economies are expected to grow at a modest pace, while emerging markets and developing economies are projected to remain relatively more resilient. The outlook continues to be constrained by weak investment momentum, elevated public debt, tighter financial conditions, and persistent policy uncertainty.

Indian Economic Outlook
Macroeconomic Landscape
Inflation and Price Dynamics
India is expected to remain among the world’s fastest-growing major economies, with GDP projected to grow by 6.6% in FY2027. Elevated energy prices and higher input costs are likely to moderate private demand, although the reduction in GST rates should support consumer spending. Reduced U.S. tariffs and the expected implementation of free trade agreements should help mitigate weaker external demand. Over the medium term, firmer domestic demand and improving export growth are expected to reinforce India’s growth momentum.

Consumer price inflation is projected to average around 4.9% in FY2027, reflecting higher global oil prices and the associated increase in transport and input costs. Inflationary pressures are likely to persist in the near term, although government measures are expected to limit the pass-through of higher global energy prices to domestic prices. As global energy markets stabilize, inflation is expected to moderate over the medium term.

Litigation Update
During FY2026, Glenmark USA continued to defend multiple antitrust and consumer protection lawsuits relating to industry-wide allegations of price- fixing, market allocation, and related conduct. The Company agreed to separate settlements with the putative direct purchaser class for USD 37.75 Mn and with state attorneys general for USD 29.63 Mn, the latter payable in annual installments over five years. The settlements are subject to the relevant court approvals and expressly state that Glenmark USA denies the allegations and does not admit liability, wrongdoing or illegality.
Russia and CIS

Russia and CIS
Glenmark’s Russia business maintained a strong secondary sales profile, recording 21% growth in Q1, 7.5% in Q2, and 15.1% in Q3, with MAT March 2026 growth of 11%. Dermatology remained a key strength: Glenmark grew faster than the covered market during the year and improved its ranking among Dermatology companies from 10th at MAT September 2025 to 9th at MAT December 2025 and 8th at MAT March 2026. The Company also maintained the second rank in the Expectorants market. Ryaltris®, ASCORIL™, and CANDIBIOTIC™ continued to sustain strong positions in their respective segments.
Europe
Glenmark Europe operations recorded revenue of INR 31,007 Mn in FY2026 as against INR 28,463 Mn in FY2025, representing growth of 8.9%. Business growth improved as the year progressed, as is evidenced by the strong second half of FY2026. This acceleration was supported by the branded business across key markets, seasonal strength in Respiratory, multiple new product launches, and improving contribution from Western Europe. The region entered FY2026 after recording more than 25% CAGR over the preceding three years and continued to gain scale across branded products.
Latin America

Latin America
The LATAM business experienced lower seasonal demand and subdued performance in selected markets during the first half, particularly Mexico and Brazil. A strong recovery followed in Q3, when the region delivered high double-digit growth, and Q4 secondary sales grew at a high single- digit rate. Multiple differentiated Respiratory launches supported the improvement. Ryaltris® was commercialized in Mexico and is planned for launch in Brazil in FY2027, while Salmeterol + Fluticasone supported the Respiratory portfolio in Brazil.
Central and Eastern European markets, including the Czech Republic, Poland, and Slovakia, continued to outperform their covered markets, aided by strong uptake of key products and new launches. Western European markets also delivered a healthy performance, particularly Germany, the Netherlands, and Italy. The branded Respiratory portfolio sustained its growth trajectory, with Ryaltris® continuing to gain market share across launched markets. Glenmark commercialized seven Respiratory products across the region during the year and plans to launch two to three additional products in FY2027.
Middle East and Africa

Middle East and Africa
The MEA region recorded double-digit secondary sales growth in major markets in Q1, followed by temporary pressure from geopolitical uncertainty and delayed launches in Q2 and Q3. The business returned to high single-digit secondary sales growth in Q4. Glenmark improved its position in Kenya to the second rank in the overall pharmaceutical market, and Ryaltris® continued to be the leading nasal spray for Allergic Rhinitis in South Africa, with healthy uptake across other key markets.
Winlevi® was launched in the United Kingdom in Q1 FY2026 and recorded strong uptake during the year. Glenmark’s partner Cosmo received a positive CHMP opinion in August 2025 and EU marketing authorization in October 2025. Commercial launches across Glenmark’s licensed EU territories are planned for FY2027, strengthening the Company’s branded Dermatology footprint in Europe.

Asia-Pacific
The APAC business strengthened progressively during FY2026. Malaysia, the Philippines, and Sri Lanka recorded high-single-digit to double-digit growth in the first half; Malaysia and Australia delivered double-digit growth in Q3; and Q4 growth was led by strong performance in Malaysia, Australia, and Sri Lanka. Glenmark continued to hold a significant position in the Dermatology and Respiratory covered markets across the region. Ryaltris® sustained strong performance and was approved and launched in China and Thailand during Q4 FY2026 through Grand Pharmaceutical and Organon, respectively.

The Emerging Markets business entered FY2026 after recording approximately 10% CAGR over the preceding three years. Revenue from Emerging Markets was INR 29,405 Mn in FY2026 as against INR 28,138 Mn in FY2025, recording growth of 4.5%.

GLENMARK’S PHILOSOPHY ON CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
At Glenmark, corporate governance is the foundation of responsible growth, sustainable value creation and stakeholder trust. It is embedded in the way we conduct our business, make decisions and create long-term value for our stakeholders.
Our governance framework goes beyond compliance and is anchored in the principles of integrity, accountability, transparency, fairness and responsible conduct. It enables effective oversight, prudent risk management and ethical decision-making while fostering innovation, resilience and operational excellence across our global operations.
The Board of Directors provides strategic guidance and oversight to ensure that the Company’s affairs are conducted in accordance with the highest standards of corporate governance and business ethics. Through a robust governance structure, clear accountability mechanisms and a culture of transparency, the Board seeks to safeguard stakeholders interests and support sustainable business performance.

As the business environment continues to evolve, Glenmark remains committed to strengthening its governance practices in line with global best practices, regulatory expectations, and stakeholders aspirations. Our governance philosophy reflects our unwavering commitment to creating enduring value while upholding the highest standards of responsibility and corporate citizenship.

The Audit Committee plays a pivotal role in strengthening the Company’s governance framework by providing independent oversight of financial reporting, internal controls, risk management and audit processes. The Committee oversees the quality and integrity of the Company’s financial statements, reviews the effectiveness of internal financial controls and monitors the adequacy of the internal audit function. It also evaluates key accounting judgments, compliance matters, related party transactions and enterprise risk management processes.

The Audit Committee maintains regular interaction with the Statutory Auditors, Internal Auditors, Cost Auditors and the management to review audit findings, significant observations and corrective actions. The Committee also reviews the independence, performance and effectiveness of the auditors and makes appropriate recommendations to the Board regarding their appointment, remuneration and continuance.
The Board has appointed M/s. Aneja Associates as Internal Auditors to conduct the internal audit of the various areas of operations and records of the Company. Further, Compliance Reports under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 and Whistle Blower Policy are also placed before the Audit Committee periodically.

Meeting(s) of the Audit Committee are also attended by the Chairman & Managing Director and the Executive Director & Global Chief Financial Officer. (2) Stakeholders' Relationship Committee
The Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee (“SRC”) plays an important role in safeguarding the interests of the Company’s security holders and strengthening stakeholders engagement. The Committee oversees various aspects relating to shareholder and investor services and ensures timely and effective resolution of stakeholders concerns.
The SRC reviews and monitors investor grievances, share transfers, transmission and transposition of securities, dematerialisation and rematerialisation requests, dividend-related matters and other investor service requests. The Committee has the mandate to review and redress shareholder grievances, including complaints relating to non-receipt of share certificates, issue of duplicate share certificates, non-receipt of Annual Reports, non-receipt of dividends and other investor-related matters.
The Committee also oversees the performance and service standards of the Company’s Registrar and Share Transfer Agent (“RTA”) and periodically reviews the effectiveness of the investor service framework. It recommends measures for enhancing shareholder experience, strengthening investor communication and improving the overall quality of investor services.

As part of its oversight responsibilities, the SRC reviews Members complaints and their resolution status on a quarterly basis. The Committee also takes note of shares and unclaimed dividends transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (“IEPF”) and monitors compliance with the applicable statutory requirements relating thereto.
Through its oversight and guidance, the Committees seeks to promote efficient investor servicing, timely grievance redressal, regulatory compliance and high standards of stakeholder satisfaction.
As on March 31, 2026, the total strength of the SRC is 3 (Three) Members, which consist of Executive, and Non-Executive Independent Directors and fulfils the criteria of composition as per Section 178 of the Act and Regulation 20 of the Listing Regulations. Independent Directors

Independent Directors
Independent Directors play a vital role in strengthening Glenmark’s governance framework by providing objective judgment, independent oversight and diverse perspectives on matters of strategic importance. Their experience across business, finance, governance, regulation, healthcare, sustainability and leadership contributes significantly to the quality of Board deliberations and decision-making.
The Independent Directors actively participate in discussions relating to strategy, risk management, financial performance, succession planning, compliance, stakeholder interests and sustainability priorities. Their independence enables constructive challenge, balanced decision-making and effective oversight of management actions.
The Board believes that Independent Directors serve as custodians of good governance and play a critical role in safeguarding the interests of all stakeholders while promoting transparency, accountability and ethical business conduct.
During the year, the Independent Directors continued to provide valuable guidance on matters relating to business transformation, governance excellence, enterprise risk management and long-term value creation. Their collective expertise and external perspectives support the Board in navigating a dynamic global business environment and strengthening stakeholder confidence in the Company.

Committee of Independent Directors
The Committee of Independent Directors serves as an important governance forum that enables Independent Directors to exchange views and exercise objective judgment on matters relating to the Company’s performance, leadership, governance and Board effectiveness, independent of the management.
The Committee comprises all the Independent Directors of the Company and functions in accordance with the requirements of Schedule IV to the Act. The meetings provide an opportunity for Independent Directors to discuss matters relating to the Company’s affairs and fulfil their oversight responsibilities in an open and constructive manner.
During the period under review, the Independent Directors met on March 12, 2026 without the presence of Non-Independent Directors and members of the management.
The Independent Directors, inter alia, reviewed and discussed:
• the performance of the Board and its Committees
• the performance of the Chairman and Non-Independent Directors
• the quality, adequacy and timeliness of information provided to the Board
• the Company’s business performance and key risks
• leadership effectiveness and succession planning and
• governance, compliance and Board composition matters

• governance, compliance and Board composition matters
The Independent Directors also provided their observations and recommendations for further strengthening governance practices and enhancing Board effectiveness.
As on March 31, 2026, the Committee comprised all 5 (Five) Independent Directors of the Company.

c. A brief on type of customers

c. A brief on type of customers
Glenmark Pharma serves a diverse and international clientele through its extensive pharmaceutical portfolio, which encompasses essential therapeutic areas including dermatology, respiratory health, oncology, cardiology, diabetes, gynecology, gastroenterology, and anti-infectives. The primary customers of the Company consist of healthcare professionals, hospitals, government wholesalers, distributors, and retail pharmacy outlets. These entities enable access to the Company’s branded, generic, and specialty pharmaceutical products, catering to a wide range of patient needs in both acute and chronic therapies. The Company functions through a strong distribution network that spans both domestic and international markets, bolstered by its subsidiaries and third-party distributors. Through this multi-channel and geographically diverse presence, the Company provides services to patients and healthcare systems throughout India and various global markets, ensuring that its offerings are in line with local healthcare demands and regulatory standards.

2. Does the entity have processes in place to avoid/ manage conflict of interests involving members of the Board? (Yes/ No) If Yes, provide details of the same:
The Company has established robust processes to identify, disclose, and manage conflicts of interest involving members of the Board and Senior Management. These processes are governed by the Glenmark Code of Conduct, which sets out clear requirements for ethical behavior, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and adherence to applicable laws and regulations. All Directors are required to disclose their interests, including directorships, shareholdings, and other potential conflict related interests in other entities, on an annual basis and whenever there is a change. In addition, Directors submit annual declarations affirming their commitment to act in the best interests of the Company and to avoid situations that may result in actual or perceived conflicts of interest.

Where an incident involving a potential conflict arises, the concerned Director abstains from participating in the discussion and decisionmaking process, in line with the Company’s governance framework and statutory requirements. Similar disclosure and affirmation requirements apply to Senior Management, who are required to confirm annually that they have not entered into any material financial or commercial transactions that could adversely impact the Company’s interests.
These measures collectively ensure transparency, independence of decisionmaking, and effective oversight, thereby safeguarding stakeholder interests.

3. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling, and disposing at the end of life, for (a) Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste and (d) other waste.
We are engaged in the manufacture and sale of pharmaceutical products. At the end of the product life cycle, plastic packaging constitutes the primary category of waste generated. In line with Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) requirements, the Company has established systems for environmentally responsible waste management in compliance with applicable pollution control regulations.
Plastic waste, including rigid, flexible, and multi‑layered packaging, is managed through authorized third‑party agencies approved by the Pollution Control Board. Recyclable waste is processed for recycling, while non‑recyclable waste is co‑processed to ensure safe disposal.
We have a centralized arrangement with authorized recyclers for the collection and recycling of e‑waste. Battery waste is returned to authorized dealers or suppliers for disposal and recycling as per regulatory requirements. Hazardous waste and other waste streams, if any, are handled through authorized vendors in accordance with applicable environmental laws.

We have obtained EPR authorization from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) under both the Brand Owner and Importer categories. 10 Health and safety management system:
a. Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? (Yes/ No). If yes, the coverage such system?
Yes. The Company has implemented an Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Management System with 100% coverage across its operations, including all manufacturing facilities in India. The system applies to both permanent employees and contractual workers. Seven out of the Company’s eight locations are certified under ISO 45001, while the remaining locations are aligned with the same OHS framework and standards.

The OHS framework is aligned with recognized occupational health and safety standards and includes processes for hazard identification, risk assessment, emergency preparedness and response, and the mandatory use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Key Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) performance indicators are monitored through a structured governance mechanism supported by periodic internal and external audits. Workplace safety is further reinforced through safety signage, emergency response systems, evacuation plans, fire safety systems, and regular training and awareness programs.
b. What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the entity?
The Company follows a structured and systematic approach to identify work‑related hazards and assess risks for both routine and non‑routine activities. Hazard identification is carried out using established tools and methodologies, including Risk Assessments (RA), Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA), Job Safety Analysis (JSA), Process Hazard Analysis (PHA), and regular plant safety inspections.

For non‑routine and high‑risk activities, a Permit‑to‑Work (PTW) system is mandatorily followed. Each permit is supported by a prior risk assessment that evaluates the nature of the task, potential hazards, severity and likelihood of risks, and surrounding working conditions. Compliance with the PTW process is monitored to ensure safe execution of such activities.
Employees and contract workers are actively encouraged to report unsafe acts, unsafe conditions, incidents, accidents, and near‑miss events through multiple reporting channels. Identified hazards are analyzed and addressed through appropriate corrective and preventive actions to minimize occupational risks.
Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment Framework:
• Department heads, in coordination with the EHS Head, are responsible for identifying hazards associated with their respective activities, equipment, and processes, and for implementing necessary risk control measures.
• Risk levels are assessed using Croner’s nomogram tool, which considers factors such as likelihood of occurrence, frequency of exposure, severity of impact, potential injury, and property damage. Based on the risk ranking, suitable engineering, administrative, and personal protective equipment (PPE) controls are applied.

• Employees across levels are involved in hazard identification and risk mitigation activities, reinforcing shared ownership and a strong safety culture.
• OHS inspections are conducted at multiple levels: daily inspections by the EHS Head with area owners, weekly inspections by plant heads, and monthly inspections by department heads. Inspection findings are periodically

5. Has the entity implemented a mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge? If yes, provide details of its coverage and implementation.
The Company has implemented Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) mechanisms across the majority of its manufacturing facilities. All Glenmark Pharmaceuticals Limited (GPL) manufacturing facilities, with the exception of Taloja and Baddi, have ZLD systems operational on site. Wastewater generated from operations at these locations is treated and reused for various applications, including utility operations and gardening, thereby significantly reducing freshwater consumption.

In addition, the Company has strengthened its wastewater safe discharge practices across its operations. In FY 2026, Glenmark achieved a key milestone by recycling and reusing 84% of the wastewater generated across its Indian operations, enabled through a combination of Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs), Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs), and ZLD systems.
To further enhance wastewater treatment and reuse, the Company has undertaken infrastructure upgrades at key sites. These include:
• Modernization of the primary treatment unit at Baddi
• Installation of Membrane Biological Reactor (MBR) based STPs at the Goa, Mahape, and Baddi facilities
• Deployment of ZLD units at the Nashik, Sikkim, and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar plants
Where ZLD systems are not currently implemented, wastewater is treated through approved treatment systems and safely discharged in accordance with applicable regulatory standards and Pollution Control Board requirements. These measures collectively ensure regulatory compliance, minimize environmental impact, and support long term water sustainability.

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
6. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements include those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.

Auditor’s Responsibility for the Audit of the Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The fair value measurement is based on the presumption that the transaction to sell the asset or transfer the liability takes place either in the principal market for the asset or liability, or in the absence of a principal market, in the most advantageous market for the asset or liability. The principal or the most advantageous market must be accessible to the Company.

2.3 Foreign currency transactions

2.3 Foreign currency transactions
Company enters into development and marketing collaborations and out-licences of the Company’s compounds or products to other parties. These contracts give rise to fixed and variable consideration from upfront payments, development milestones, sales-based milestones and royalties. Income dependent on the achievement of a development milestone is recognised when it is highly probable that a significant reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognised will not occur, which is usually when the related event occurs. Sales-based milestone income is recognised when it is highly probable that the sales threshold will be reached.
Functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which the Company operates whereas presentation currency is the currency in which the financial statements are presented. Indian Rupee is the functional as well as presentation currency for the Company.

Functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which the Company operates whereas presentation currency is the currency in which the financial statements are presented. Indian Rupee is the functional as well as presentation currency for the Company.
Foreign currency transactions are recorded at the exchange rates prevailing at the date of such transactions. Monetary assets and liabilities as at the balance sheet date are translated at the rates of exchange prevailing at the date of the balance sheet. Gain/loss arising on account of differences in foreign exchange rates on settlement/translation of monetary assets and liabilities are recognised in the statement of profit and loss, unless they are considered as an adjustment to borrowing costs, in which case they are capitalised along with the borrowing cost attributable to qualifying assets.
Sales-based royalties on a licence of intellectual property are not recognised until the relevant product sale occurs. If the time between the recognition of revenue and payment from the customer is expected to be more than one year and the impact is material, the amount of consideration is discounted using appropriate discount rates.

2.5 Property, plant and equipment
Recognition and measurement
Items of property, plant and equipment are measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses, if any. Cost comprises of purchase price (after deducting trade discount/rebate) / cost of construction, non-refundable duties and taxes, borrowing costs, other expenditure that are directly attributable to the acquisition of the asset. The cost of self-constructed assets includes the cost of materials and other costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to a working condition for its intended use.
Company receives revenue for supply of goods to external customers against orders received. The majority of contracts that Company enters into relate to sales orders containing single performance obligations for the delivery of pharmaceutical and consumer healthcare products. The average duration of a sales order is less than 12 months.

Revenue from sale of goods is recognised when control of the goods is transferred to the customer, there are no unfulfilled obligations, the amount of revenue can be reliably measured, and it is probable that future economic benefits associated with the transaction will flow to the Company. The point at which control gets transferred is determined by each customer arrangement, but generally occur on delivery to the customer.
When parts of an item of property, plant and equipment have significant cost in relation to total cost and different useful lives, they are accounted for as separate items (major components) of property, plant and equipment.
Profits and losses upon disposal of an item of property, plant and equipment are determined by comparing the proceeds from disposal with the carrying amount of property, plant and equipment and are recognised within “other income/expense" in the statement of profit and loss.
Revenue represents net invoice value including fixed and variable consideration. Variable consideration arises on the sale of goods as a result of discounts and allowances given and accruals for estimated future returns and rebates. Revenue is not recognised in full until it is highly probable that a significant reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognised will not occur.

The cost of replacing part of an item of property, plant and equipment is recognised in the carrying amount of the item if it is probable that the future economic benefits embodied within the part will flow to the Company, its cost can be measured reliably and it has a useful life of at least twelve months. The costs of other repairs and maintenance are recognised in the statement of profit and loss as incurred.

2.6 Borrowing costs
Borrowing costs primarily comprise interest on the Company's borrowings. Borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset are capitalised during the period that is necessary to complete and prepare the asset for its intended use or sale. De-recognition of intangible assets
Intangible assets are de-recognised either on their disposal or where no future economic benefits are expected from their use or disposal. Losses arising on such de-recognition are recorded in the statement of profit and loss, and are measured as the difference between the net disposal proceeds, if any, and the carrying amount of respective intangible assets as on the date of de-recognition.

• Fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI): Assets that are held for collection of contractual cash flows and for selling the financial assets, where the assets’ cash flows represent solely payments of principal and interest, are measured at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI). Movements in the carrying amount are taken through OCI, except for the recognition of impairment gains or losses, interest income and foreign exchange gains and losses which are recognised in the statement of profit and loss. When the financial asset is derecognised, the cumulative gain or loss previously recognised in OCI is reclassified from equity to the statement of profit and loss and recognised in other income/ expenses. Interest income from these financial assets is included in other income using the effective interest rate method.
De-recognition of financial assets
A financial asset is derecognised only when
 the Company has transferred the rights to receive cash flows from the financial asset or

 the Company has transferred the rights to receive cash flows from the financial asset or
 retains the contractual rights to receive the cash flows of the financial asset, but assumes a contractual obligation to pay the cash flows to one or more recipients.
Where the entity has transferred an asset, the Company evaluates whether it has transferred substantially all risks and rewards of ownership of the financial asset. In such cases, the financial asset is derecognised. Where the entity has not transferred substantially all risks and rewards of ownership of the financial asset, the financial asset is not derecognised.
• Fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL): Assets that do not meet the criteria for amortised cost or FVOCI are measured at fair value through profit or loss. A gain or loss on a debt investment that is subsequently measured at fair value through profit or loss and is not part of a hedging relationship is recognised in the statement of profit and loss and presented net in the statement of profit and loss within other income/expenses in the period in which it arises. Interest income from these financial assets is included in other income.

Where the entity has neither transferred a financial asset nor retains substantially all risks and rewards of ownership of the financial asset, the financial asset is derecognised if the Company has not retained control of the financial asset. Where the Company retains control of the financial asset, the asset is continued to be recognised to the extent of continuing involvement in the financial asset.
Interest income from financial assets
Interest income from debt instruments is recognised using the effective interest rate method. The effective interest rate is the rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash receipts through the expected life of the financial asset to the gross carrying amount of a financial asset. When calculating the effective interest rate, the Company estimates the expected cash flows by considering all the contractual terms of the financial instrument (for example, prepayment, extension, call and similar options) but does not consider the expected credit losses.

Defined benefit plans

Defined benefit plans
A defined benefit plan is a post-employment benefit plan other than a defined contribution plan. The Company’s net obligation in respect of an approved gratuity plan, which is a defined benefit plan, and certain other defined benefit plans is calculated separately for each material plan by estimating the ultimate cost to the entity of the benefit that employees have earned in return for their service in the current and prior periods. This requires an entity to determine how much benefit is attributable to the current and prior periods and to make estimates (actuarial assumptions) about demographic variables and financial variables that will affect the cost of the benefit. The benefit is discounted to determine the present value of the defined benefit obligation and the current service cost. The assessment of the probability of future taxable profit in which deferred tax assets can be utilized is based on the Company’s latest approved budget forecast, which is adjusted for significant non-taxable profit and expenses and specific limits to the use of any unused tax loss or credit. If a positive forecast of taxable profit indicates the probable use of a deferred tax asset, especially when it can be utilised without a time limit, that deferred tax asset is usually recognised in full. The recognition of deferred tax assets that are subject to certain legal or economic limits or uncertainties is assessed individually by management based on the specific facts and circumstances.
For accounting period beginning on or after 1 April 2026, when an entity breaches any covenant of a long-term loan arrangement on or before the end of the reporting period with the effect that the liability becomes payable on demand, it classifies the liability as current, even if the lender agreed, after the reporting period and before the approval of the financial statements for issue, not to demand payment as a consequence of the breach. An entity classifies the liability as current because, at the end of the reporting period, it does not have the right to defer its settlement for at least 12 months after that date.

However, an entity classifies the liability as non-current if the lender agreed by the end of the reporting period to provide a period of grace ending at least 12 months after the reporting period, within which the entity can rectify the breach and during which the lender cannot demand immediate repayment.

NOTE 26 - EMPLOYEE POST- RETIREMENT BENEFITS
The following are the employee benefit plans applicable to the employees of the Company.
a) Gratuity (defined benefit plan)
In accordance with the applicable laws, the Company provides for gratuity, a defined benefit retirement plan (“the Gratuity Plan”) covering eligible employees. The Gratuity Plan provides for a lump sum payment to vested employees on retirement, death, incapacitation or termination of employment of amounts that are based on salary and tenure of employment. Liabilities with regard to the gratuity plan are determined by actuarial valuation.

Risk Exposures:
The Company is exposed to various risks in providing the above benefit which are as follows:
Interest Rate risk: The plan exposes the Company to the risk of fall in interest rates. A fall in interest rates will result in an increase in the ultimate cost of providing the above benefit and will thus result in an increase in the value of the liability (as shown in financial statements).
Liquidity Risk: This is the risk that the Company is not able to meet the short-term gratuity payouts. This may arise due to non availability of enough cash/cash equivalent to meet the liabilities or holding of illiquid assets not being sold in time.
Salary Escalation risk: The present value of the defined benefit plan is calculated with the assumption of salary increase rate of plan participants in future. Deviation in the rate of increase of salary in future for plan participants from the rate of increase in salary used to determine the present value of obligation will have a bearing on the plan's liability.
Demographic Risk: The Company has used certain mortality and attrition assumptions in valuation of liability. The Company is exposed to the risk of actual experience turning out to be worse compared to the assumption.

Regulatory risk: Gratuity benefit is paid in accordance with the requirements of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (as amended from time to time). There is a risk of change in regulations requiring higher gratuity payouts (e.g. Increase in the maximum limit on gratuity of ` 20,00,000).

The Company permits encashment of leave accumulated by their employees on retirement and separation. The liability for encashment of privilege leave is determined and provided on the basis of actuarial valuation performed by an independent actuary at the date of the balance sheet.
Risk Exposures:
The Company is exposed to various risks in providing the above benefit which are as follows:
Interest Rate risk: The plan exposes the Company to the risk of fall in interest rates. A fall in interest rates will result in an increase in the ultimate cost of providing the above benefit and will thus result in an increase in the value of the liability (as shown in financial statements).
Liquidity Risk: This is the risk that the Company is not able to meet the short-term gratuity payouts. This may arise due to non availability of enough cash/cash equivalent to meet the liabilities or holding of illiquid assets not being sold in time.

Salary Escalation risk: The present value of the defined benefit plan is calculated with the assumption of salary increase rate of plan participants in future. Deviation in the rate of increase of salary in future for plan participants from the rate of increase in salary used to determine the present value of obligation will have a bearing on the plan's liability.
Demographic Risk: The Company has used certain mortality and attrition assumptions in valuation of liability. The Company is exposed to the risk of actual experience turning out to be worse compared to the assumption.
Asset liability mismatching or Market risk: The duration of the liability is longer compared to duration of assets, exposing the Company to market risk for volatilities/fall in interest rate.
Investment risk: The probability or likelihood of occurrence of losses relative to the expected return on any particular investment.

(a) In January 2014, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) issued a demand notice of ` 12.24 Crs as overcharging liability of product "Doxovent 400 mg tab" for the period February 2010 to May 2013. The notice also envisaged a payment of ` 3.33 Crs towards interest @15% p.a. on the overcharged amount up to 31 January, 2014. The Company had filed a petition under Article 32 with the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India (Hon’ble Court), challenging the issue of the above mentioned demand notice on various grounds. This petition was tagged along with other petitions filed by other pharmaceutical companies, pending before Hon’ble Court relating to the inclusion criteria of certain drugs including "Theophylline" in the schedule of the DPCO, 1995. The Hon’ble Court passed an ad-interim order stating that no coercive steps be taken against the Company towards the said demand. Whilst the matter was pending before the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in October 2015,
